title: The 128-lane wall
subtitle: Padding waste ran under one percent until every shape used all of its 128 lanes, then climbed past 95 percent on a 22-million-item load test; the fix was structural
technologies: Capacity engineering, backpressure and load testing

stats.label: tokens in the 22-million-item load test that found the wall
padding waste in the two-GPU window after the fix
phases of changes to widen the lane id

lede: My broker packs prompts of similar length into lanes so that a batch pads as little as possible. Each lane has a target length, items go to the lane that wastes the least, and a new lane opens when the waste would be too high. The first version gave each shape 128 lanes, because the lane id was a byte and 128 seemed like plenty. A load test showed exactly what plenty was worth. As the run went on, every shape reached a hundred percent lane pressure, meaning every one of its 128 lanes was in use and no new lane could open.
quote: Tuning the waste threshold could not help, because the threshold only decides when to open a lane, and no lane could be opened.
evidence: Performance diagnosis: traced padding waste of 95%+ on a 22-million-item load test to a structural budget of 128 lanes per shape, a capacity limit that no threshold tuning could fix.
Token-aware scheduling: widened the lane id to 16 bits across 8 phases of changes, raising the budget to 2,048 lanes so the pressure-scaled waste threshold could work.
GPU inference optimisation: padding waste at 0.421% in the two-GPU window after the fix, with average lane pressure at 22% instead of 100%.
author: Corey James
